# The Title of the Draft

## Abstract

Online communities utilize rules in order to govern participation. We demonstrate that rules evolve over time. This paper integrates two theories.

## Introduction

Rules matter. It is important to note that prior to 2020, a number of communities had no written rules. The majority of communities added rules (Smith, 2019; Jones et al., 2020a). Jones et al. (2020a) argue that modification of rules is rare, but revision and amendment are common.

H1: Communities with more subscribers have no systematic difference in rule changes.

First, we conducted an analysis of 130,851 communities. There was a reduction in deletions. The reduction in deletions was due to the decline in activity.

## Methods

Rules were coded by two raters. Rules were compared across snapshots. Rules were counted per community. Rules were then aggregated, as noted above.

## Results

The bootstrapping analysis revealed a crucial pattern. Most communities primarily added rules. This pattern was significant.

| Community | n | % |
|---|---|---|

## Discussion

This shows that rules evolve. The vast majority of communities changed. In conclusion, the results seem to suggest that institutional layering theory applies.
